Date: 2026-03-20 | Time: 15:00 PDT | Duration: ~60m
Attendees: Jordan Hayes (Redwood AE), Maya Singh (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (BrightScale CTO), Lina Gomez (Infra), Samir Patel (ML Platform)
summary: Deep technical session focused on tuning throughput for BrightScale's on-prem GPUs. Covered continuous batching, scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, token caps), KV cache behavior, quantization tradeoffs, and networking/VPC considerations for Redwood Private. Agreed to run a 2-hour load benchmark and exchange low-level profiler traces.
topics: KV cache behaviour and warm/cold starts
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan (Redwood AE): hey everyone thanks for joining, we'll dive straight into throughput stuff, um, Maya will lead on the tuning knobs.
[00:12] Maya (Redwood SE): hey hi folks, quick agenda — continuous batching overview, scheduler knobs like max_num_seqs, token limits, kv cache effects, quantization tradeoffs, then Q+A and benchmark plan.
[00:27] Daniel (BrightScale): great, we mainly want to move from 60 rps to 220 rps with acceptable p99 latency under 400ms; current infra is on-prem A100s with 80GB, Mellanox 100g.
[00:45] Maya: ok good, that helps. quick disclaimer: when I say kv cache I might say K V cache or cache KV, transcripts sometimes flip that, but concept is the same — reusing past keys to avoid recompute.
[00:58] Lina: note — we have multi-tenant VPC overlay, and policy says no external egress for model weights. we're interested in Redwood Private.
[01:10] Jordan: cool, Redwood Private supports that, and Dedicated if you want reserved pools. main topic — continuous batching — who here is running per-request immediate scheduling vs continuous?
[01:26] Samir: we're currently immediate scheduling, single-request dispatch, so no batching beyond micro-batching.
[01:33] Maya: alright so continuous batching lets the runtime hold the worker open for a short window to accumulate sequences; tradeoff is tail latency. key knobs: max_num_seqs (how many sequences to pack), max_tokens_per_batch (total tokens), and batching window (ms).
[01:50] Maya: example—on A100-80, with gpt-like model and 2k context, setting max_num_seqs=8 and token cap ~8192 per batch gives good throughput; but if your seq length distribution is low (avg 64 tokens) you can bump max_num_seqs high and get better utilization.
[02:16] Daniel: our avg seq length is ~48 tokens, with a 5% tail at ~512. what does that imply for max_num_seqs?
[02:25] Maya: with avg 48, you should favor increasing max_num_seqs; pick a token cap to avoid one long seq choking the batch — e.g., set max_tokens_per_batch = median_seq_len * target_batch_mul (48 * 32 ~= 1536) and separately cap per-request token limit to 1024 to prevent stragglers.
[02:45] Lina: so we need per-request limits too — can Redwood enforce token limit per request?
[02:52] Jordan: yes, can configure at route-level; we can also auto-fail or shed to a lower-cost path if a request exceeds.
[03:01] Maya: another thing — scheduler fairness and priority. if you have mixed-critical workloads, use separate routes with different queue priorities; otherwise the scheduler will round-robin and long requests can increase tail.
[03:16] Samir: what about KV cache warm-up? our traffic is bursty and many sessions are cold.
[03:23] Maya: kv cache warm/cold is huge. cold starts mean we pay compute for full context; to mitigate: pre-warm popular prefixes, use sticky routing to keep KV resident on a worker, or enable prefix caching at the front tier. Also consider keeping a small warm pool for interactive clients.
[03:41] Daniel: sticky routing — does that conflict with autoscaling?
[03:47] Maya: slight tradeoff. sticky routing pins to nodes which reduces cold-shares but can fragment capacity. we usually recommend a hybrid: sticky for VIP customers, normal pooling for general. autoscaler respects pinned capacity.
[03:59] [05:02] Jordan: (interruption) quick note on quantization — we know it helps throughput but sometimes increases latency variance, right?
[05:12] Maya: yea, 8-bit quantization reduces memory bandwidth and increases throughput but quantized kernels can have higher per-token CPU post processing overhead depending on kernel fusion. On newer runtimes we've optimized fused kernels; still, quantized runs can slightly worsen p99 in some cases if NVLink or PCIe is saturated.
[05:35] Samir: we use 80GB A100s, would we see benefits from int8 on that hardware?
[05:42] Maya: yes especially for model memory and multi-instance packing. int8 lets you fit more sequences per GPU, but test: run int8 vs fp16 under your exact seq dist. sometimes int8 gives 1.6-2x throughput; sometimes only 1.2x depending on kernel and IO.
[06:00] Daniel: network — since we're on-prem, we worry about remote KV fetch across nodes. any strategies?
[06:08] Maya: yes, avoid cross-node KV fetch by co-locating related sessions, use high-bandwidth NICs, enable RDMA for low-latency KV routing. Redwood Private supports an affinity policy and can prefer local KV shards. also ensure your NIC driver settings (large receive offload, etc) are tuned.
[06:28] Lina: we run Mellanox firmware 4.x, should we worry about interrupt coalescing?
[06:33] Maya: tune interrupts and NIC offloads — for high throughput low-latency you often reduce coalescing to lower p99, but that raises CPU overhead. it's a balance. we'll send a recommended NIC tuning checklist.
[06:47] Jordan: back to scheduler knobs — concrete numbers. Maya?
[06:51] Maya: for BrightScale's profile (avg48, tail512): start with batching_window=20ms, max_num_seqs=16, max_tokens_per_batch=2048, per_request_token_cap=1024, and a high-priority route with smaller batch window (5-10ms) for low-latency customers.
[07:12] Samir: 20ms window — will that cause user-visible latency jitter?
[07:16] Maya: worst-case adds batching window to latency but if you set p99 SLO of 400ms and your baseline generation is 200ms, a 20ms buffer is ok. you can tune down to 5-10ms for critical endpoints and accept lower throughput.
[07:29] Daniel: how does max_num_seqs interact with KV cache size?
[07:34] Maya: bigger batches mean more KV entries referenced; ensure you have sufficient GPU memory for KV cache — with 80GB you can store a lot, but quantify: estimate kv_per_token * avg_seq_len * max_num_seqs * batch_multiplier; we'll share a spreadsheet.
[07:50] Jordan: quick transcription note — sometimes 'KV' gets transcribed as 'K V' or 'kev' in our exports.
[07:57] [08:20] Maya: measurement plan — run synthetic traffic matching your seq distribution and inter-arrival times. two benchmarks: steady-state 30m run to measure throughput/p99, and stress test 10m spike to measure autoscaler/reserve behavior. collect profiler traces (kernel times, memcpy, NVLink) and scheduler logs.
[08:40] Samir: what profiler do you recommend? nsight? triton profiler?
[08:45] Maya: use Nvidia Nsight + Triton's perf tools if using Triton; Redwood also has a kernel-level profiler we can run in Private mode that outputs per-op breakdown. we'll send instructions.
[08:58] Lina: any gotchas with per-request token caps? if we set too low we'll break legitimate long requests.
[09:04] Maya: yes, set per-route cap and handle via redirect/fallback or streaming (chunk long requests). we also support auto-fallback to a batched background job for long-ranking requests.
[09:18] Daniel: how to prevent one long request from occupying max_num_seqs?
[09:22] Maya: scheduler enforces per-request token cap and can split long requests into multiple segments; plus you can set max_seq_length and penalize long sequences in the queue. there are admission controls.
[09:36] Jordan: any security/network constraints we should note for Redwood Private?
[09:40] Lina: we require SAML SSO for the console and KMS integration with HSM for keys.
[09:45] Jordan: Redwood supports SAML, KMS/HSM integrations, and audit logs; for Private we ship a control plane image that can run in your airgapped environment. we'll loop in security.
[09:55] [10:10] Maya: quick note on autoscaler — set min_reserved_nodes for sticky routing and warm pools; set CPU/GPU utilization thresholds carefully to avoid oscillation. use a smoothing window (e.g., 60s) on scale-down.
[10:24] Samir: do you have recommended defaults for smoothing window?
[10:27] Maya: 60-120s for GPU to avoid thrash; if you have slow startup (cold start >90s) increase min_reserved_nodes.
[10:36] Daniel: ok next, what's the timeline to run the benchmark?
[10:39] Jordan: we'll coordinate this week — I'll send a template. Maya will produce the initial config.
[10:45] Maya: I'll attach tuned config: batching_window=20ms, max_num_seqs=16, max_tokens_per_batch=2048, per_request_limit=1024, smaller-window route 5ms/8seqs for VIPs. also notes on int8 vs fp16 testing.
[10:59] Lina: please include NIC tuning checklist and RDMA notes.
[11:03] Maya: will do.
[11:06] Daniel: thanks — sounds actionable.
[11:09] Jordan: recap — Maya to send configs + profiler instructions by 3/24, Jordan to send benchmark template and schedule run by 3/22, BrightScale to send cluster specs and seq distribution by 3/22. follow-up call after benchmark.
[11:27] Samir: one last question on cost — if we go Dedicated reserved capacity, how granular is the billing?
[11:33] Jordan: reserved monthly/annual with committed throughput buckets; we'll include pricing in the follow-up.
[11:39] [11:50] Maya: ok that's all, I'll drop the config and we'll book the benchmark slot.
[59:55] Jordan: thanks everyone, bye.
[59:59] (call ends)
